Industry News: Australia urged to wean off imported fossil fuels amid global supply shocks

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (808 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Grattan Institute report calls on government to ‘seize’ opportunity to cap diesel tax credits, introduce EV subsidies for less wealthy’ and build ‘clean’ refineries.
  • Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast.
  • Capping lucrative diesel tax handouts to big business, building fresh “clean” refineries and targeting electric vehicle subsidies to less wealthy people could save Australians thousands of dollars in fuel per year, according to a major new report calling on the government to reduce reliance on imported fossil fuels.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grattan Institute report calls on government to ‘seize’ opportunity to cap diesel tax credits, introduce EV subsidies for less wealthy’ and build ‘clean’ refineries.

Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast.

Capping lucrative diesel tax handouts to big business, building fresh “clean” refineries and targeting electric vehicle subsidies to less wealthy people could save Australians thousands of dollars in fuel per year, according to a major new report calling on the government to reduce reliance on imported fossil fuels.

The Grattan Institute, one of the nation’s most respected thinktanks, has warned Australia imports too much of its fuel, and that the country must brace for more global supply shocks – like that from the war in Iran. Under a initiative already attracting criticism from business groups, Grattan urged diesel handouts to mining and primary industries be curbed in favour of incentives for electric trucks and a huge expansion of the EV charging network.

Sources indicate that “Relying on fuel imports during an era of benign international relations and dependable strategic partners was a passable strategy. But in a more dangerous and unpredictable world, it is no longer tenable,” the report, released on Sunday, warned.

Sources indicate that “Australia should expect the coming decades to be less stable than the past one. This means bracing, and preparing, for more oil shocks.”.

According to recent reports, australia imports 97% of its liquid fuel. Grattan’s fuel plan report, Fuelling the Future, warns this “leaves us dangerously exposed to supply disruptions and price hikes”.

It argues that the US-Israel war in Iran has driven up inflation and cost Australians nearly $18bn, and the federal government directly at least $3bn, creating an opportunity the government “should seize” to boost fuel security.

Very little liquid fuel is produced or refined in Australia, with only two domestic oil refineries. But rather than boosting that number, Grattan states Australia should lower its reliance on imported fuels and fossil fuels generally by shifting towards EVs, including an ambitious target of 650,000 electric trucks nationwide by 2050.

That alone would cut Australia’s diesel use by 5bn litres a year, Grattan forecast. The report also calls for the fuel tax credit program – which costs Australia billions each year – to be capped at $35m per corporate group annually.

According to recent reports, the biggest user of that program – which refunds taxes on fuel for machinery and heavy vehicles travelling on private, rather than public, roads – is the mining sector. The fuel tax credit scheme has become a political hot-button issue, with major business campaigning for it to be preserved amid calls for it to be reined in.

Tania Constable, CEO of the Minerals Council of Australia, rejected the Grattan proposal.

According to recent reports, “Australia does need stronger fuel security, but making diesel more expensive for regional industries won’t create a single extra litre of fuel, build a refinery or improve supply-chain resilience. Instead, it would increase costs for miners, farmers, freight operators and regional businesses, with those costs ultimately flowing through to Australian households,” she said.

“If the goal is greater energy security, then Australia should be focused on increasing domestic production, expanding refining capacity and building more resilient supply chains – not making essential fuel more expensive.”.

But the Grattan report notes capping the scheme would save the government $3bn annually, and hasten the electrification of the mining sector – which it noted would help the mining sector in the long run.

Recent findings suggest that the report also recommends the government invest $1.1bn in a national network of chargers for EVs, as well as provide $2.4bn in vouchers for trucking firms to buy electric trucks. It calls for federal vehicle standards to be boosted to incentivise cleaner cars, as well as a restructuring of EV subsidies “to target people least able to afford them”.

Labor is widely expected to restrict current EV subsidies in next month’s mid-year economic update, as the government searches for budget savings.

In other areas of fuel use, Grattan notes Australia produces no “clean” jet fuel, and recommends the government direct $6bn to the first generation of so-called “clean refineries” to make that fuel.

Grattan indicates these refineries could provide nearly 10bn litres of clean jet fuel per year by 2050, but notes that it could cost $100bn to build them all, and that importing clean jet fuel would be cheaper.

But it argues that $6bn – the savings generated from just two years of capping the fuel tax credits to mining companies – would cover a quarter of the cost of the first five refineries, kickstarting the sector and providing fuel security in future supply shocks.

“Historically, making fuel meant making fossil fuels. But in an age of electrification and clean fuels, Australia now has more options,” the report mentioned.

#58842. 6 handy ways you can use your old mini PC

6 handy ways you can use your old mini PC

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1177 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, building or upgrading a PC isn't as thrilling as it once was, especially with the AI takeover.
  • The cool part is that this little box can become your retro gaming console, host your media library, or even serve as a dedicated AI coding workstation.
  • While your old mini PC may not handle the latest AAA games, it could make a great retro gaming console.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, building or upgrading a PC isn't as thrilling as it once was, especially with the AI takeover. If RAMageddon has left a bitter taste in your mouth, an old mini PC you have lying around might be worth putting to use. Sure, it won't get magically faster, but replacing it has certainly gotten expensive.

The cool part is that this little box can become your retro gaming console, host your media library, or even serve as a dedicated AI coding workstation. But a lot of what you can do with it does depend on what's under the hood. Some projects require only free software, while others may require some hardware and patience. So here are six ways to get one working again.

While your old mini PC may not handle the latest AAA games, it could make a great retro gaming console. Batocera is a free, Linux-based operating system you can use to turn it into a dedicated machine for playing Nintendo, Sega, and PlayStation classics.

It is fairly easy to get started. Download Batocera's PC image, flash it onto a USB stick, and boot your mini PC from it. This lets you test the operating system without replacing Windows, though you may need to disable Secure Boot or enroll Batocera's signing key to get it running. If Windows uses BitLocker, make sure you have your recovery key before changing Secure Boot settings.

Once it's up and running, you can connect the mini PC to your TV via HDMI, pair a compatible controller, and add your legally acquired games. Batocera arranges everything in a console-style interface, so you can easily navigate your library without a keyboard.

Industry observers note that performance will vary depending on hardware. Many older mini PCs can handle 8-bit and 16-bit games, but the PlayStation 2 and GameCube may be a bit of a challenge. Another way to play compatible PC games on your TV is Steam's Major Picture Mode, if your machine is powerful enough. But don't count on a controller to make up for an outdated processor and integrated graphics.

An old mini PC can also be a dedicated home for your movie and music collection. Plug it into your TV, install Kodi, and you have a media center to browse and play stored content locally. If you want to view your library on several devices, Plex and Jellyfin can stream your files to compatible TVs, phones, and tablets over your home network.

Sources indicate that however, you should consider hardware restrictions first. A video played in its native format typically uses less processing power than one converted on the fly for an incompatible device. That process, known as transcoding, can strain older processors, especially with 4K content.

Plex also requires a Plex Pass or Remote Watch Pass for remote personal video streaming on affected apps, unless the server owner already has Plex Pass. Local streaming remains free. Jellyfin doesn't charge for remote streaming, but you have to set it up yourself.

You can also turn the mini PC into a network-attached storage (NAS) device. Attach an external SSD or hard drive and share files on the home network with software like OpenMediaVault. It's a practical solution for storing family photos, documents, and backups without relying on paid cloud storage.

But you still have to consider drives, electricity, and occasional maintenance. With storage prices off the charts, buying additional drives could be costly. Plus, while a NAS can hold backups, it shouldn't be the only place you keep anything notable. One dusty old hard drive with all your family photos isn't exactly a good backup proposal.

If you're at a party and everyone wants to add a song to the queue, passing your phone around can get tedious. An old mini PC can handle it. Pair it with a touchscreen and speakers, and you've got the makings of a digital jukebox for your living room or home bar.

Industry observers note that apps like Jukiora can turn a Windows mini PC into a music station, with album art and a touchscreen interface for browsing songs. Alternatively, TouchGroove also lets guests queue songs from their phones via a QR code. This means everyone can add to the playlist without passing the phone around.

It has been revealed that you'll need your own music library to play your own songs, since neither app includes a music collection. Both Jukiora and TouchGroove offer seven-day free trials, followed by a one-time purchase. If you don't already have a touchscreen around, it may also increase the price. It's still a pretty fun way to put a mini PC to use that may otherwise be sitting in retirement collecting dust.

Recent findings suggest that if you already have security cameras in your home, you can use your old mini PC to record the footage. Try Frigate, an open-source network video recorder (NVR) that works with compatible IP cameras to store footage locally instead of relying on a manufacturer's cloud recording service.

In a recent development, the program can also detect objects like people and vehicles in camera footage using AI. So finding the footage of someone walking up to your front door or a car pulling into your driveway is much easier than sifting through hours of footage. You can even set how long recordings are kept, depending on available storage space.

The only catch here is that not every hardware setup will play ball. Frigate requires processors that support AVX and AVX2 instructions, ruling out many older Celeron, Pentium, and Atom chips. With multiple cameras, hardware-accelerated video decoding and an appropriate object detector can also make a big difference. You'll also need ample storage space and working knowledge of Docker to get it up and running.

With AI coding assistants so popular right now, your aging mini PC could have another role to play. Although powerful hardware can make a massive difference when running AI models, you can still experiment on some older but capable hardware.

Sources indicate that one easy way to get started is Ollama. You can download smaller language models and run them directly on your computer, letting you ask questions, summarize text, or even play around with a chatbot without sending every prompt to the web. After installing it, you can use local models without shelling out a single cent. Obviously, you can't expect an old processor with limited RAM to perform as well as a modern AI workstation.

Sources indicate that anthropic's coding assistant, Claude Code, can analyze project files, modify code, and run commands, with cloud-based models handling the heavy lifting of AI processing. It comes with Claude Pro, priced at $20 per month in the US (billed monthly), or you can pay for it separately based on API usage.

It has been revealed that claude Code can also connect to locally hosted models via Ollama, though running a good coding model on older hardware is a different story. According to Ollama, Meta's Llama 3.2 1B model is a 1.3 GB download.
